hook.text: Clear the first SQL screen, and the follow-ups change. Rank these. Compare each day with the one before. Keep only the latest row for each customer. Nearly all of it comes down to one tool: the window function.

plan.text: There are twenty questions here. We'll work through twelve of them on real queries, then take the last eight at speed.

window-in.text: Start with what a window actually is.

window.text: Question one. What is a window function, and how does the over clause work?

window-group.text: Group by collapses rows. Six sales by region become two totals: North four twenty-five, South six forty.

window-over.text: A window function keeps every row. Sum over, partitioned by region, writes each region's total beside its sales: six rows in, six rows out.

window-parts.text: Inside over, you can say three things: which rows share a window, their order inside it, and the frame around the current row.

partition.text: Question two. What does partition by do, versus order by? Partition by splits the rows into groups, and the window starts over in each one. Order by sets the order inside a group, which is what a ranking needs.

partition-rank.text: Rank, partitioned by region and ordered by amount, starts again at one for South. North's two fifty and South's three twenty both come first.

rank-in.text: Which brings us to ranking, and to ties.

rank.text: Question three. How do row number, rank, and dense rank differ?

rank-ties.text: Look where the scores tie. Three people have eighty-eight, and four have eighty-five.

rank-three.text: Row number gives every row its own number, so a tie is broken arbitrarily. Rank lets ties share a number, then skips: eight, eight, eight, then eleven. Dense rank shares without the gap: eight, then nine.

topn.text: Question four. How do you return the top N rows per group? Number the rows inside each category, then keep the first N. With row number, you get exactly two per category. Emma and Ulysses tie at three ten, and only one of them makes it.

topn-rank.text: Use rank instead, and both tied books come back: five rows.

qualify.text: Question five. What is qualify? It filters on a window function the way having filters on an aggregate, with no wrapping query. DuckDB, Snowflake and BigQuery support it.

frame-in.text: Now the part people most often get wrong: the frame.

frame.text: Question six. What is a window frame, and how do rows and range differ?

frame-def.text: The frame is the slice of rows the function can see, counted from the current one. Here, two payments fall on the same day.

frame-rows.text: Rows counts physical rows, so the running total climbs one payment at a time: a hundred, three fifty, four twenty-five.

frame-range.text: Range goes by the order by value, so both payments on the second day come in together. Both get four twenty-five.

default.text: Question seven. What is the default frame? Add order by with no frame, and you get range, from the start to the current row. So sum over order by day is a running total, not the total. Leave out order by, and every row gets six oh five.

last.text: Question eight. What's the last value gotcha? With that default frame, the window ends at the current row, so last value just returns the row's own amount. Widen the frame to unbounded following, and every row gets the real last day: one eighty.

running-in.text: Two calculations every analyst gets asked to write.

running.text: Question nine. How do you compute a running total? An ordered sum, with the default frame: a hundred, three fifty, four twenty-five, six oh five, and on to four thousand two hundred fifty-five by the twenty-fourth.

moving.text: Question ten. How do you compute a moving average? Average over an explicit rows frame, the two rows before and the current one. The first two days have less behind them, so they average one value and then two. A centered average uses one preceding and one following.

latest-in.text: And two patterns that turn up in almost every take-home.

latest.text: Question eleven. How do you keep only the latest row for each user? Number each user's rows from the newest, and keep row one. User one has three rows. Only the newest, team, survives.

spine.text: Question twelve. How do you fill gaps in a date series? Sales skip the second and the fifth, so those days are simply missing, and a chart draws straight over them.

spine-fix.text: Generate every day with generate series, left join the sales onto it, and turn the missing amounts into zeros with coalesce.

rapid-in.text: That's the heavy lifting done. Eight more, at speed.

r-lag.text: Lag reads a value from an earlier row, and lead from a later one. Day over day change is the amount minus its lag.

r-ntile.text: N tile splits ordered rows into equal buckets. Twenty-four customers make four quartiles of six. Split them five ways, and the first buckets each take an extra row.

r-where.text: Can a window function go in where? No. Windows are computed after where, group by and having, so DuckDB refuses. Filter in an outer query, or with qualify.

r-recursive.text: A recursive CTE is a common table expression that refers to itself. It starts from anchor rows and keeps joining back on itself until nothing new turns up. Here it walks an org chart from the CEO down five levels.

r-bucket.text: Date trunc snaps a timestamp to the start of its day, week or month. January's twenty-four days fall into four weeks.

r-pivot.text: To pivot, wrap a case in a sum for each new column: one row per region, with the quarters side by side.

r-unpivot.text: To unpivot, union all one select per column, and the wide table turns long again.

r-percent.text: And percent rank runs from zero for the first row to one for the last. Cume dist is the share of rows at or below this one, so it never reaches zero.

next.text: Results like these usually end up in a spreadsheet, and that's where the next round goes. Next: Excel and spreadsheets.
